newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish opinion split on EU Amsterdam Treaty - poll.
newsitem.headline: Danish opinion split on EU Amsterdam Treaty - poll.

text.p: Danish opinion is divided on the European Union's Amsterdam Treaty reforms, with those in favour, against and unsure running almost neck-and-neck, an opinion poll showed on Wednesday.

The Sonar Institute survey, published in the leading daily newspaper Jyllands-Posten, asked how Danes would vote in a referendum. It found 35 percent would accept the treaty, 34 percent would reject it, and 31 percent were unsure or did not intend to vote.
Previous polls have shown a narrow majority of Danes in favour of the treaty, agreed at a European Union summit in Amsterdam in June, with almost half of samples undecided.
Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen has said that he will ask Danes to vote on the Amsterdam Treaty changes early next year, but has set no date as yet.
Danes traditionally have a lukewarm attitude to Europe. They shocked their fellow EU members by flatly rejecting the Maastricht Treaty on closer European cooperation in a referendum in 1992.
They only voted to ratify the treaty the following year on condition that Denmark opt out of economic and monetary union, a joint defence structure, cross-border policing and a common asylum policy.

EU leaders decided at Amsterdam to leave the Western European Union defence grouping independent of the union, to grant Britain and Ireland opt-outs from a plan to lift internal border checks, to make job creation a formal EU goal, and to increase cooperation in foreign policy and asylum policy.
The summit left key institutional reforms to be taken early next century.
